analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture and sale of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban the manufacture and sale of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in February 2015 and never received a vote or a hearing before the Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess ammunition magazines, drums, or belts that hold more than 10 rounds. Magazines already owned when the law took effect would stay legal, and police, retired officers, nuclear-material security workers, and licensed testers would be exempt. New magazines would have to carry a serial number and date, devices used in crimes could be seized, and federal grants could fund buy-back programs that pay people for turning large-capacity magazines in. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the people who would gain are those exposed to mass shootings and other gun violence, since high-capacity magazines let a shooter fire many rounds without reloading, and reducing their availability is aimed at limiting casualties in such attacks; police departments would also benefit from fewer such weapons on the street. The bill's design spreads the benefit over time: people who already own large-capacity magazines keep them, so the restriction mainly works by cutting off the supply of new devices as old ones age out.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People exposed to mass shootings and gun violence

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess any ammunition magazine, belt, drum, or similar device that holds or can be readily converted to hold more than 10 rounds, the high-capacity magazines used in many mass shootings.
It requires new magazines to carry a serial number and manufacture date engraved or cast on the device, and makes devices used in knowing violations subject to seizure and forfeiture.
It allows cities and states to use federal Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grants to pay people for turning in large-capacity magazines under buy-back programs.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on firearms and magazine manufacturers and dealers, who would lose the ability to make and sell a legal product line, and on gun owners, who could no longer buy, sell, or transfer magazines holding more than 10 rounds and would face criminal penalties and forfeiture for possessing new ones. People who already owned such devices would pay nothing beyond the option to sell them.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and some gun owners

drawbacks.text: Possession would become a federal crime for devices acquired after enactment, exposing otherwise law-abiding gun owners to felony penalties for magazines that are commonplace and millions of which remain in circulation.

Existing devices would remain legal without any registration or surrender requirement, so the ban's effect would be gradual and dependent on old magazines wearing out or being voluntarily turned in through buy-backs.
Because the restriction keys off a 10-round capacity, gun owners could still buy and combine many 10-round magazines, limiting how much the law slows a determined shooter's rate of fire.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is fewer deaths and injuries when shootings occur, since magazines holding more than 10 rounds have figured in many of the deadliest attacks; the grandfathering and buy-back provisions make the bill more workable than a confiscation, and the carve-outs for police and nuclear-plant security address the most legitimate law-enforcement needs. The main costs fall on gun owners, who would face federal felony exposure for manufacturing, selling, or transferring devices that are commonplace today, and the grandfathering means the law's protective effect would arrive only slowly as pre-existing magazines age out of circulation. On balance it is a real but incremental restriction whose burden is concentrated on the firearms trade and on owners who would have to stop replacing worn-out or lost high-capacity magazines.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice in the Senate and sent to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never voted on it, so it simply expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on February 5, 2015, joined by 16 Democratic cosponsors including Dianne Feinstein, Richard Durbin, Chuck Schumer, and Elizabeth Warren.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.

No further action appears in the bill's record: the Judiciary Committee never held a markup or vote, and the Senate never debated it. Bills that receive no action die when a Congress ends, and this one ended on January 3, 2017.
Every cosponsor was a Democrat; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers and sellers of high-capacity magazines kept an unrestricted civilian market, and gun owners kept the ability to buy and sell them; no restrictions took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Magazine makers, sellers, and gun owners

for.name: 16 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors, including Blumenthal, Feinstein, Warren, Gillibrand, Whitehouse, Carper, Durbin, Reed, Boxer, Murphy, Franken, Markey, Schumer, Hirono, Murray, and Kaine

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never held a markup or vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman during the 114th Congress, never scheduled the bill for committee action.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed bans on large-capacity magazines and pressed lawmakers to reject them.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans controlling the Senate and its Judiciary Committee, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill bans manufacturing, selling, and transferring new magazines holding more than 10 rounds, ending a legal product line for domestic makers and importers. Manufacturers would retain a lawful testing-and-experimentation carve-out but lose the civilian market.
Dealers could no longer sell large-capacity magazines to civilians, cutting off a steady accessory business. Police and other exempt buyers would remain a smaller, narrower market.

People who already owned large-capacity magazines keep them with no registration or surrender required, and the bill funds buy-backs for those who want to give them up. But owners could no longer buy, sell, or hand down new ones, and possession of a post-enactment device would carry criminal penalties and forfeiture.
